body:
Law, policy, institutions and programmes serve different purposes

India's response to cybersecurity challenges does not rest on a single law or government body. Different instruments establish offences, provide legal rules for evidence, guide national security priorities, support institutional coordination and improve preparedness.

A competitive-exam question may describe a provision, institution or initiative and ask the learner to identify its purpose. The key is to recognise whether it is a law, policy, reporting arrangement, technical agency or training programme.

The Information Technology Act, 2000

The Information Technology Act, 2000 is a central legal framework for matters involving electronic records, electronic transactions and specified computer-related offences. It also provides the statutory basis for important cybersecurity institutions.

The following provisions illustrate the distinctions needed for basic objective questions.

ProvisionPrincipal subjectIllustrative distinction
Section 66CIdentity theftFraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or unique identification feature
Section 66DCheating by personation using a computer resourceCheating by impersonating another person through a communication device or computer resource
Section 70Protected systemsProtection of specified computer resources and the concept of CII
Section 70ACritical information infrastructure protectionStatutory basis for designation of the national nodal agency, NCIIPC
Section 70BCyber incident responseStatutory basis for CERT-In's national functions

Identity theft and cheating by impersonation

Section 66C and section 66D address different aspects of unlawful conduct. Section 66C concerns the fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's specified identification features. Section 66D concerns cheating through personation using a computer resource or communication device.

For example, using another person's password dishonestly may raise an issue of identity theft under section 66C. A person who pretends to represent a trusted authority through digital communication and thereby cheats a victim may raise an issue under section 66D. The precise offence in a real case depends on the facts and the legal elements proved. A single incident may involve more than 1 offence.

National Cyber Security Policy, 2013

The National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 was issued by the Department of Electronics and Information Technology under the then Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. Its purpose is to guide the development of a secure and resilient cyberspace for citizens, businesses and government.

The policy addresses the protection of information and information infrastructure, cybersecurity preparedness, cooperation among stakeholders, institutional capacity, workforce development and the protection of critical information infrastructure.

The policy recognises that effective cybersecurity requires multiple organisations to cooperate. A problem may affect citizens, businesses and government services simultaneously, so prevention and response cannot be confined to a single office.

The National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 is a policy framework. It is not itself the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, a police investigation agency or the legislation defining every cybercrime.

Cyber Surakshit Bharat

Cyber Surakshit Bharat was launched by MeitY on 19 January 2018 in association with the National e-Governance Division and industry partners.

Its purpose is to strengthen cybersecurity awareness and capacity among government Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) and frontline information-technology staff. Its 3 guiding principles are Awareness, Education and Enablement.

The initiative contributes to preparedness and improved practices in public administration. It does not register FIRs, investigate citizens' financial fraud complaints or replace CERT-In's statutory functions.

The national cybercrime policy and response framework

The Ministry of Home Affairs coordinates important aspects of national cybercrime response through I4C. The framework includes the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, the 1930 helpline and the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System.

These arrangements connect citizens' reports with financial institutions and the relevant law-enforcement agencies. State and Union Territory police retain their responsibilities for investigation under criminal law.

In contrast, CERT-In, under MeitY, performs national cyber incident-response functions. NCIIPC, under NTRO, has the specialised role of protecting critical information infrastructure. The distinction between the 2 national frameworks is not a division between important and unimportant incidents; it is a distinction between different legal and institutional functions.

Digital evidence and personal data protection

Cybersecurity also intersects with laws governing evidence and personal information.

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in force from 1 July 2024, addresses the treatment of electronic and digital evidence. Its sections 61 and 63 are particularly relevant to the recognition and admissibility of electronic records.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 concerns the processing and protection of digital personal data. Its focus is different from the prosecution of cybercrime. A personal-data protection obligation does not replace the process of reporting financial fraud or investigating an unlawful intrusion.

Status of the DPDP framework at the content cutoff

The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified with phased commencement arrangements. According to MeitY's announcement dated 14 November 2026, the Consent Manager registration framework came into effect on 13 November 2026.

Other important provisions concerning the rights of Data Principals, obligations of Data Fiduciaries, and the Board's inquiry and penalty processes were scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027. Therefore, as at 16 November 2026, notification of the framework did not mean that every substantive requirement had already commenced.

A Data Principal is the individual to whom personal data relates. A Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. A registered Consent Manager is intended to help Data Principals give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.

Cybercrime law addresses specified unlawful conduct. Evidence law governs proof in legal proceedings. Personal-data protection law governs specified processing of personal data. These areas may overlap in practice, but they are not interchangeable.

Putting the framework together

Consider a suspected unlawful change to a government database containing personal information. The department must address the technical incident and assess applicable CERT-In reporting obligations. If the facts suggest criminal conduct, the appropriate police authority may investigate. Digital records may be relevant evidence. Depending on the facts and the commencement of applicable provisions, personal-data protection obligations may also arise.

Thus, a single event can engage several legal and institutional systems without those systems performing the same function.

Prelims focus

  • IT Act section 66C: identity theft; section 66D: cheating by personation using a computer resource.
  • National Cyber Security Policy: 2013.
  • Cyber Surakshit Bharat: MeitY initiative launched on 19 January 2018.
  • CERT-In directions: 28 April 2022; specified Annexure I incidents must be reported by covered entities within 6 hours.
  • I4C: Ministry of Home Affairs; CERT-In: MeitY; NCIIPC: NTRO.
  • Trap: The DPDP framework has phased commencement; as at 16 November 2026, several major provisions were scheduled for 13 May 2027.

Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026; legal and policy status stated at that cutoff.]

pictures.alt: Six cyber problems lead to distinct Indian response institutions, linked by evidence preservation, harm containment and essential-service continuity.
pictures.caption: India's cyber response links citizen reporting, technical coordination, criminal investigation and infrastructure protection.

title: India's Cybercrime Laws, National Cyber Security Policy and Preparedness Framework
